q: Ethanol is heated with concentrated hydrochloric acid in the presence of anhydrous zinc chloride. The organic product is:
x: ZnCl₂ helps HCl replace the –OH group: C₂H₅OH + HCl → C₂H₅Cl + H₂O. Ethene and ethoxyethane are dehydration products made with concentrated H₂SO₄, not HCl/ZnCl₂.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CHClCH(CH₃)₂ is:
x: The longest chain has 4 carbons. Numbering from either end puts the substituents at 2 and 3, so the tie is broken alphabetically: chloro comes before methyl and gets the lower number. 3-Chloro-2-methylbutane numbers from the wrong end; '2-methyl-3-chloro' breaks the alphabetical order.

q: Which reaction gives 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCl, as the main product?
x: HCl adds to (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ by Markovnikov's rule, putting Cl on the carbon with two methyl groups. SOCl₂ keeps the chlorine where the OH was, giving 1-chloro-2-methylpropane; but-1-ene gives 2-chlorobutane; free-radical chlorination of 2-methylpropane gives mainly the primary chloride because there are nine primary H to one tertiary H.

q: 4.6 g of ethanol is converted completely into bromoethane with PBr₃: 3C₂H₅OH + PBr₃ → 3C₂H₅Br + H₃PO₃. What mass of bromoethane is formed? (C₂H₅OH = 46, Br = 80)
x: 4.6/46 = 0.10 mol ethanol gives 0.10 mol C₂H₅Br (ratio 3:3). M(C₂H₅Br) = 24 + 5 + 80 = 109, so 0.10 × 109 = 10.9 g. Dividing by 3 (reading the ratio as 3:1) gives 3.6 g; multiplying by 3 gives 32.7 g.

q: The correct IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br is:
x: The longest chain is three carbons (CH₂Br–C–CH₃) with two methyls on C2. Numbering from the CH₂Br end gives the locants 1,2,2; from the other end they are 2,2,3, so the first set wins and 3-bromo is wrong. The butane names belong to isomers with a different skeleton.

q: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₃H₆Cl₂?
x: On a three-carbon chain the two Cl atoms can be at 1,1 (CHCl₂CH₂CH₃), 1,2, 1,3 and 2,2 (CH₃CCl₂CH₃): four isomers. Missing a geminal isomer (both Cl on one carbon) gives 3; counting 2,3 or 3,3 separately repeats 1,2 and 1,1.

q: The SN2 reaction of hydroxide ions with bromomethane, CH₃Br, has an overall order of:
x: SN2 is one step in which OH⁻ and CH₃Br collide, so rate = k[CH₃Br][OH⁻], first order in each and second order overall. First order is the SN1 rate law, where only the alkyl halide appears.

q: An optically active sample of 3-bromo-3-methylhexane, a tertiary alkyl halide, is hydrolysed by water through the SN1 mechanism. The alcohol formed is:
o: Only the isomer with inverted configuration
Only the isomer with the same configuration
A racemic mixture, because the flat carbocation is attacked equally from both faces
Not formed, because tertiary halides do not undergo substitution
x: The C–Br bond breaks first to give a planar sp² carbocation; water can attack either face equally, giving both mirror-image alcohols in equal amounts. Complete inversion is the result of SN2 back-side attack.

q: The rate of SN2 reactions falls in the order CH₃Br > CH₃CH₂Br > (CH₃)₂CHBr > (CH₃)₃CBr. The main reason is that:
o: Tertiary carbocations are less stable than methyl carbocations
The C–Br bond is much stronger in tertiary bromides
Tertiary bromides are more polar than bromomethane
Alkyl groups crowd the back of the carbon atom and hinder the approach of the nucleophile
x: In SN2 the nucleophile must reach the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group; each extra alkyl group blocks this path. Carbocation stability belongs to SN1 and actually runs the other way (tertiary most stable).

q: Bromoethane can give either ethanol (substitution) or ethene (elimination) with KOH. Which conditions favour elimination?
o: Dilute aqueous KOH at room temperature
Dilute aqueous KOH, cooled in ice
x: In ethanol, with a high concentration of base and heat, OH⁻ (and C₂H₅O⁻) acts as a base and removes a β-hydrogen, giving CH₂=CH₂. Aqueous, dilute, cool conditions favour OH⁻ acting as a nucleophile and give ethanol.

q: Bromoethane is heated with potassium cyanide in ethanol. The main organic product is:
x: CN⁻ is a nucleophile and replaces Br⁻: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN + Br⁻, adding one carbon to the chain. CH₃CN forgets that the cyanide carbon is added rather than swapped for a carbon of the ethyl group.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃, is heated with concentrated alcoholic KOH. The major organic product is:
x: Alcoholic KOH with heat causes elimination. A β-H can go from a CH₃ (giving 2-methylbut-1-ene) or from the CH₂ (giving (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃); the more substituted alkene is the major product (Saytzeff rule). The alcohol would form with aqueous KOH; 3-methylbut-1-ene would need the double bond away from the C–Br carbon.

q: Bromoethane is warmed with magnesium turnings in dry ether. The product is:
x: Magnesium inserts between carbon and bromine: C₂H₅Br + Mg → C₂H₅MgBr, a Grignard reagent, kept in solution by the ether. Butane would be the Wurtz product with sodium; C₂H₅OMgBr forms only if the reagent meets oxygen or an alcohol.

q: Any Grignard reagent, RMgX, reacts with methanal, HCHO, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The product is always a:
x: R adds to the carbon of HCHO, giving RCH₂OMgX and then RCH₂OH; the carbinol carbon has two H atoms, so the alcohol is primary. Other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones tertiary; carboxylic acids come from CO₂.

q: Phenylmagnesium bromide, C₆H₅MgBr, reacts with propanone, CH₃COCH₃, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The product is:
x: The phenyl group adds to the carbonyl carbon of propanone, which already carries two CH₃ groups; hydrolysis gives the tertiary alcohol C₆H₅C(CH₃)₂OH. 1-Phenylpropan-1-ol would come from propanal, an aldehyde.

q: 0.10 mol of ethylmagnesium bromide reacts completely with excess methanal, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. What mass of alcohol is obtained? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
x: C₂H₅MgBr + HCHO then H₃O⁺ gives CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, propan-1-ol (M = 60); 1:1 ratio, so 0.10 × 60 = 6.0 g. 4.6 g forgets that methanal adds a carbon and uses ethanol (46); 7.4 g uses a four-carbon alcohol.

q: For the same alkyl group, the ease of forming a Grignard reagent with magnesium in dry ether follows the order:
x: Magnesium must break the C–X bond, and the C–I bond is the weakest, so iodides react most readily and chlorides least. Choosing R–Cl first confuses bond polarity with bond strength.

q: Which compound CANNOT be used to prepare a stable Grignard reagent by reaction with magnesium in dry ether?
x: A Grignard reagent is destroyed by any acidic hydrogen. In BrCH₂CH₂OH the –OH of the molecule itself would protonate the C–Mg carbon as soon as it formed. The other three have no O–H or N–H group; aryl and secondary halides form Grignard reagents normally.
